sections.title: Warm-up
sections.prompt: Name three people in your family and one word that describes each of them.
sections.lede: Say each line aloud once. This section is not scored.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: These are the three things you will be able to do by the end of the lesson.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Introduce the people closest to you with possessives and the verb sein.

blocks.text: Use mein or meine before a family member: mein Bruder, meine Schwester, meine Eltern. The possessive ending follows the gender and number of the noun, not the person who owns it.
To describe someone, use sein plus an adjective: Mein Bruder ist freundlich. After sein, the adjective has no ending. For age, German uses the verb sein, not haben: Sie ist zwanzig Jahre alt.

blocks.title: Family words are often irregular
blocks.text: Learn the plural with the noun: der Bruder → die Brüder, die Schwester → die Schwestern, das Kind → die Kinder.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

rows: Meine Schwester ist zwanzig Jahre alt.

items: The adjective after sein does not take an ending.
Use alt for people and things; use "Jahre alt" for age.
Eltern, Geschwister and Großeltern are plural words.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: Listen once, then read the example aloud.

items.exampleEn: My brother is ten years old.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short, focused sound work. Play each item and repeat it twice.

items.hint: Stress the second syllable: fa-MI-lie, with a long i.
Start with sch, then a short e: SHVES-ter.
The u is long: BROO-der. The final -er is soft.

blocks.text: German family words are often used without possessive articles when the relationship is clear: "Das ist meine Schwester" is common, but "Meine Schwester ist Ärztin" is more natural than repeating the name.
Many German families are small, and "Geschwister" covers brothers and sisters together. If you want to ask someone about their family, "Hast du Geschwister?" is a natural, polite question.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Possessives and sein
sections.lede: The possessive ending depends on the noun that follows it.

blocks.text: Add an adjective after sein without an ending: Mein Bruder ist freundlich. Do not say "mein freundlicher Bruder" at A1 unless you are describing the noun before a statement.

sections.tip: Use sein for age and descriptions: Er ist zwölf. Sie ist freundlich.

sections.title: Choose the right answer
sections.lede: Choose the answer that fits the sentence or the rule.

exercises.explanation: Schwester is feminine, so use meine.
Age uses sein in German: Er ist zehn Jahre alt.
Bruder is masculine, so use mein, and the description uses ist.
Eltern is plural, so the possessive is meine.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Introduce two family members and describe each one with one adjective.

model.de: Das ist meine Schwester. Sie ist sehr freundlich. Mein Bruder ist zehn Jahre alt.
model.en: This is my sister. She is very friendly. My brother is ten years old.

tips: Use meine before feminine nouns and mein before masculine or neuter nouns.
After ist, do not add an ending to the adjective.
Use "Das ist …" to introduce someone, then a second sentence to describe them.
